summaries.example: Imagine two friends choosing whether to help clean a shared art room. If both help, the room becomes tidy and both finish quickly. Each friend might still be tempted to let the other do the work. If both make that choice, the room stays messy. Game theory helps us study how each person’s best choice depends on what the other person does.
summaries.summary: Game theory is a way to study situations where people, animals, companies, or governments make choices while reacting to one another. It does not mainly study games for fun. It studies strategy: planning while thinking about what others may do. A player’s preferences can be represented by utility, a number or ranking that shows which outcomes the player likes better. A game may have one move for each player, or many moves in sequence. Tables show the results of combinations of choices. Branching diagrams show who moves when and what each player knows. A Nash equilibrium is a set of plans in which no player would gain by changing plans alone. But a Nash equilibrium is not always the best result for everyone. In the Prisoner’s Dilemma, each person has a reason to choose the safer personal option, yet both end up worse off than they would have been through cooperation. Game theory also studies imperfect information, uncertainty, repeated games, coordination, social rules, and commitment. These ideas help explain why cooperation sometimes succeeds, sometimes fails, and sometimes needs support from institutions or shared expectations.
key_ideas: Game theory studies choices that affect one another.
A result can happen even when no one wanted it.
A player’s best move depends on the other players’ possible moves.
Games can be shown with tables or branching diagrams.
The Prisoner’s Dilemma shows how individually sensible choices can produce a worse result for everyone.
Rules, promises, repeated interaction, and commitment can change what choices make sense.
summaries.why_it_matters: Many everyday situations involve choices that depend on other people: sharing work, following traffic rules, competing, making agreements, or deciding whether to trust someone. Game theory gives us careful tools for seeing why a good plan for one person may not lead to a good result for a group. It can also help us think about how changing information, rules, timing, or future interactions can make cooperation easier.

important_terms.definition: A situation in which people or other decision-makers choose while considering how others may respond.
A person, group, animal, company, or other decision-maker in a game.
What a player prefers, or how good an outcome is for that player in the model.
A plan that says what a player will do in every situation that might arise.
An outcome where no player can do better by changing alone, while the others keep their plans.

questions_to_think_about: When does helping others also help you?
Can a promise work if nobody can make you keep it?
Why might two people choose a result that is worse for both?
How could a rule help people cooperate?

summaries.example: Two firms are deciding whether to keep prices high by limiting production. If both keep the agreement, both may earn strong long-term profits. Each firm, however, can gain briefly by producing more while the other keeps its limit. If both reason this way, the agreement collapses. In a one-shot model, defection may be the only Nash equilibrium. If the firms expect many future interactions, punishment and reputation may support cooperation, although the outcome depends on information, the expected endpoint, and whether mistakes can be detected.
summaries.summary:
Game theory analyzes interacting choices among agents whose preferred actions depend on what other agents do or are expected to do. The theory models agents using preferences, utility functions, available strategies, information, and payoffs. In the technical use of “rationality,” an agent can rank outcomes, connect actions with likely results, and select an available action that best serves its modeled preferences. This does not by itself claim that actual people always deliberate consciously, nor does it settle broader philosophical debates about rationality, morality, emotion, or empathy.

Games may be represented in strategic form, usually by a matrix listing payoffs for combinations of strategies, or in extensive form, usually by a tree showing sequence, decision points, information, and outcomes. These representations are not interchangeable when timing and information matter. In finite perfect-information games, backward induction analyzes later choices first and works backward. A strategy profile is a Nash equilibrium when no player can gain by changing alone. Nash equilibrium is useful but often incomplete: non-zero-sum games can have several equilibria, and equilibrium analysis may ignore what players would do at unreached decision points. Subgame-perfect equilibrium requires equilibrium behavior in every subgame and therefore rules out some incredible off-path plans.

The Prisoner’s Dilemma illustrates a conflict between individual incentives and efficiency. Each player has a strictly dominant action, so mutual defection is the unique Nash equilibrium under the standard payoffs. Yet mutual cooperation gives both higher payoffs. This inefficiency does not require selfish psychology; utility can represent anything a player cares about, and the dilemma is fixed,
key_ideas: Game theory distinguishes parametric choices, where the environment is passive, from strategic choices, where other agents anticipate and respond.
Ordinal utility records preference order; cardinal utility also represents preference intensity relevant to choices under risk.
Strategic-form matrices summarize strategy combinations, while extensive-form trees preserve timing and information.
Nash equilibrium is a stability concept, but it may leave several equilibria or fail to select the outcome that seems most reasonable.
Subgame perfection addresses threats or plans that would not be rational if an off-path decision point were reached.

The Prisoner’s Dilemma separates individual incentives from collective efficiency: mutual defection is an equilibrium, while mutual cooperation is Pareto superior but unstable without additional support.
summaries.why_it_matters: Game theory matters because strategic dependence appears throughout economics, politics, biology, social life, and philosophy. It helps distinguish a bad outcome caused by the structure of incentives from one caused by inaccurate assumptions about preferences or information. The framework can illuminate cooperation, coordination, bargaining, institutional rules, reputation, commitment, and learning. At the same time, the entry emphasizes that equilibrium concepts are analytical tools rather than automatic predictions of actual behavior. Applying them well requires careful attention to payoffs, timing, beliefs, uncertainty, mistakes, and evidence about how agents behave.

important_terms.definition: A formal study of strategic interaction: situations in which the outcome of one agent’s choice depends on the choices or expected choices of others.
A representation of an agent’s preference ordering or welfare ranking; ordinal utilities need not measure psychological pleasure or comparable quantities between people.
A complete plan specifying an action at every decision point where a player might have to act.
A strategy that gives a player a better outcome than another strategy for every possible strategy of the opponent.
A profile of strategies such that no player can improve their payoff by changing strategy alone, given the others’ strategies.
A game representation that records players, available actions, order of play, information, and outcomes in a branching structure.
An equilibrium that remains a Nash equilibrium in every subgame, including situations that would occur off the actual path of play.
A change in the structure of a game that makes more efficient outcomes possible or more likely.

questions_to_think_about: Should a theory of rationality predict only payoff-maximizing behavior, or should it include moral or team-centered reasoning?
When several Nash equilibria exist, what could select one: communication, focal points, norms, learning, or risk concerns?
Why can a commitment improve an outcome by restricting a player’s future options?
How should models represent mistakes, uncertain beliefs, and heterogeneous human behavior?
When does repeated interaction support cooperation, and when does uncertainty instead produce conflict?

summaries.example: Suppose four students are planning a group presentation. Each student would like everyone to prepare, because the final presentation will be better. But each student also has a short-term reason to do less work and hope the others finish it. If everyone follows that temptation, the group may receive a poor grade. If the students meet repeatedly, divide jobs clearly, and know that unfinished work will affect future trust, cooperation may become easier. The important point is that the same people can face different incentives when the rules and expectations change.
summaries.summary:
Game theory studies situations in which several decision-makers affect one another through their choices. The decision-makers are players, and the possible results are outcomes. A player’s preferences can be represented by utility: a ranking or number system showing which outcomes are better from that player’s point of view. Utility does not have to mean money or pleasure. It can represent whatever matters in the model, and the entry discusses different ways of interpreting it.

A game is strategic when a player must consider how another player may respond. A strategy is a complete plan for possible situations, not merely the move chosen right now. Games can be represented by matrices or by trees. A strategic-form matrix shows what happens for each combination of strategies, while an extensive-form tree shows the order of actions and what players know. These differences matter because a game that looks the same in a matrix may have different timing or information structures.

Game theorists use solution concepts to analyze possible results. A Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies where no player can improve by changing alone. It is a kind of stability, not necessarily fairness, morality, or social efficiency. The Prisoner’s Dilemma is a famous example. Each player has a reason to choose the action that protects their own payoff, even though both would receive more from mutual cooperation. Communication alone may not help if promises cannot be enforced. In other games, several equilibria may exist, so analysts consider ideas such as focal points, refinements, or subgame perfection. Subgame perfection checks whether planned behavior would still make sense at every later part of a game.

The entry also examines repeated games, uncertainty, mixed strategies, commitment,,
key_ideas: Game theory examines interdependence: what is sensible for one player depends on expectations about others.
“Rationality” in game theory is a technical idea about ranking outcomes, connecting actions to results, and choosing among available options.
A strategy is more than a single move because it covers possible future situations.
Matrices hide some information about timing, while game trees can show order, knowledge, and choices at different points.
A Nash equilibrium can be stable without being best for the group.
The Prisoner’s Dilemma shows why cooperation may be valuable but difficult when agreements cannot be enforced.
summaries.why_it_matters: Game theory gives us a way to ask precise questions about cooperation and conflict without assuming that every disagreement is caused by bad character. A result may come from the timing of choices, missing information, weak promises, or incentives that no individual can change alone. Understanding these structures can help students think more clearly about teamwork, competition, rules, trust, and institutions. It also teaches caution: a model’s conclusions depend on how the players, preferences, information, and available actions are described.

important_terms.definition: A situation where each person’s result depends partly on the choices of other people who are also choosing.
A decision-maker in a game, such as a person, team, business, or government.
A ranking or numerical representation of how much a player prefers possible outcomes.
A full plan for what a player will do in every possible situation in the game.
A strategy profile in which no player can improve their result by changing alone.
A game in which players move one after another and a tree records the possible paths.
A game in which a matrix lists the payoff for each combination of players’ strategies.
A result that is better for at least one player and no worse for any other player than another result.

questions_to_think_about: Is a stable outcome always a good outcome?
How does knowing the order of moves change a game?
Why might communication fail to solve a Prisoner’s Dilemma?
Can a social rule be useful even if some people disagree with it?
How might future meetings change what students or businesses choose today?
